docs.contenu:
🎯 Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
- Understand what an argumentative essay is and how it differs from a balanced essay.
- Build a clear thesis statement and defend it with strong, ordered arguments.
- Support each argument with reasons, examples and evidence.
- Answer a counter-argument and write a convincing conclusion.

🔍 Warm-up
Imagine a friend says, "Reading books is a waste of time." How would you convince them they are wrong? You would not just say "You are wrong." You would give reasons: books build vocabulary, spark imagination, and reduce stress. That is exactly what an argumentative essay does: it defends ONE clear position with solid reasons.

I. WHAT IS AN ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY?
📘 Rules and definitions
An argumentative essay defends a single, clear point of view and tries to persuade the reader that it is right. Unlike a for-and-against essay, it does not stay neutral: from the first paragraph, the writer takes a side.
Its structure is:
- Introduction with a clear thesis statement.
- Body paragraphs, each defending one main argument.
- A counter-argument paragraph (the opposing view) that the writer then answers.
- A conclusion that restates the position with force.

📝 Grammar patterns and usage
An argumentative essay uses:
- opinion language: I firmly believe, in my opinion, there is no doubt that;
- strong linkers: firstly, moreover, furthermore, in addition, therefore;
- concession language for the counter-argument: admittedly, it is true that, although some may claim.
These structures give the essay a confident, formal voice.

✏️ Worked examples
Weak thesis: "Sport is good." (too vague)
Strong thesis: "Daily physical exercise should be part of every school timetable because it improves health, concentration and teamwork."
The strong version names the position AND previews the main arguments. Compare two more: the weak "Pollution is bad" says nothing precise, while the strong "Cities must invest in clean transport because pollution threatens health, harms the climate and lowers the quality of daily life" both takes a side and lists the reasons the essay will develop. A precise thesis is a promise to the reader, and every paragraph that follows must keep it.

II. BUILDING AND ORDERING ARGUMENTS
📘 Rules and definitions
Each body paragraph follows the PEE pattern:
- Point: the topic sentence stating one argument.
- Evidence/Explanation: reasons, facts or examples that prove it.
- (Link): a sentence that connects back to the thesis or on to the next point.
Order your arguments from strong to strongest, so the essay grows in power.

🛠️ Writing method
Plan before you write:
1. Read the question and decide your position clearly.
2. Write a one-sentence thesis.
3. List three arguments; keep the best for last.
4. Add one example or reason to each argument.
5. Prepare one counter-argument and your answer to it.
6. Write, then reread for linkers, grammar and spelling.

✏️ Worked examples (a model outline)
Question: "Should young people volunteer in their community?"
- Thesis: Yes, because it develops skills, helps others and builds character.
- Argument 1: it teaches responsibility and teamwork.
- Argument 2: it supports people in real need.
- Argument 3 (strongest): it shapes caring, active citizens.
- Counter-argument: it takes time from studies; Answer: a few hours a week is enough and even improves motivation.
- Conclusion: restate that volunteering is valuable for everyone.

III. COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, INTRODUCTIONS AND CONCLUSIONS
📘 Rules and definitions
- A counter-argument shows you understand the other side. You state it fairly, then refute it (prove it weaker than your position).
- The introduction moves from a general idea (a hook) to your specific thesis.
- The conclusion restates the thesis in new words, summarises the arguments, and may end with a call to action or a final thought.

📝 Grammar patterns and usage
Useful frames:
- Introduction hook: "In today's world, many people wonder whether..."
- Refuting: "Although some argue that..., this view ignores the fact that..."
- Conclusion: "For all these reasons, it is clear that...", "In the light of these arguments, ..."

👀 Notes
One argument per paragraph. If a paragraph contains two big ideas, split it. Each topic sentence should announce a single point, and every following sentence should support that one point only. This keeps your essay easy to follow.

⚠️ Common mistakes
- Sitting on the fence: an argumentative essay must take a clear side.
- A vague thesis that names no arguments.
- Giving opinions with no supporting reason or example.
- Forgetting the counter-argument, which makes the essay one-dimensional.
- Introducing a brand-new argument in the conclusion.
- Repeating the introduction word for word in the conclusion.

⭐ To remember
- Take ONE clear side and state it in the thesis.
- One argument per paragraph, ordered from strong to strongest.
- Support every point with a reason or example (PEE).
- Include and answer a counter-argument.
- End by restating the thesis with force, not with new ideas.

🔗 Applications
The argumentative essay is a core task in the Baccalauréat exam. The same skills help you write opinion articles, motivation letters and debate speeches, and they train you to think logically and defend your ideas with confidence.

enonce.question: Write an argumentative essay of about 150 words to support the following statement: 'Social media has a positive impact on society.' Use at least two arguments to justify your point of view.
Which of these is a strong thesis statement? A) 'Technology is interesting.' B) 'Schools should teach coding because it develops logical thinking and prepares students for future jobs.'
Name the three parts of the PEE paragraph pattern used in argumentative writing.
Sort these expressions into OPINION language or CONCESSION language: 'I firmly believe', 'admittedly', 'there is no doubt that', 'it is true that some people'.

Write an argumentative essay of about 200 words to argue against the following statement: 'Homework should be abolished in schools.' Use at least two counterarguments to challenge the statement and support your opinion.
Turn this weak thesis into a strong one: 'Reading is good.'
Write a complete PEE body paragraph (Point, Evidence, Link) defending the idea that 'students should learn a musical instrument'.
Write a counter-argument and a refutation for the thesis 'Homework should be reduced'. Use a concession linker.

Order these three arguments for the thesis 'Cycling to school is beneficial' from WEAKEST to STRONGEST: (a) it is cheaper than the bus, (b) it keeps students healthy and fit, (c) it saves a little time on short trips.
Write an introduction (3 sentences) for an argumentative essay on 'Should plastic bottles be banned in schools?' Move from a general hook to a clear thesis.

Write an argumentative essay of about 250 words to discuss the following statement: 'Technology in the classroom enhances learning more than traditional teaching methods.' Use at least three arguments to support your view and address a potential counterargument.

Write a full argumentative essay (about 180-220 words) defending ONE clear position on: 'Should students be allowed to use the internet freely during lessons?' Include a thesis, two arguments, a counter-argument with a refutation, and a conclusion.

Write a full argumentative essay (about 180-220 words) defending ONE clear position on: 'Is it better to read printed books than digital ones?' Support your view with at least two arguments and answer one opposing point.

Read this weak conclusion and rewrite it properly for an argumentative essay whose thesis is that 'volunteering benefits young people': 'So volunteering is good. Also, young people should recycle more and eat healthy food.'
